NARA 22-U.R.MUCK. OGIS ADR +Chief FOIA Officers Meeting 2 Feb 2022

On January 16, 2022 6:54 PM I nest that same email (Attachment A) to ogisopenmeeting@nara.gov; alina.semo@nara.gov; bobak.Talebian@usdoj.gov; kirsten.mitchell@nara.gov; Vanita.Gupta19@usdoj.gov; debra.wall@nara.gov; martha.murphy@nara.gov; sheela.portonovo@nara.gov; carrie.mcguire@nara.gov; teresa.brady@nara.gov; dwaine.bacon@nara.gov; jessica.hartman@nara.gov; christa.lemelin@nara.gov; garym.stern@nara.gov.

4.	NARA, DOJ, and agencies across the Federal Government have been citing unlawful language wrt OGIS dispute resolution requiring requesters to contact the Agency FPL first:

 “If you are unable to resolve your FOIA dispute through our FOIA Public Liaison, the Office of Government Information Services (OGIS), the Federal FOIA Ombudsman’s office, offers mediation services to help resolve disputes between FOIA requesters and Federal agencies.”

Requested Records.

I am respectfully seeking as individual files  records in NARA’s custody only from January 15  2022 to present records related to said January 16, 2022 emails and any emails or other OGIS or DOJ correspondence relating to OGIS dispute resolution services as follows:

1.	Records of receipt, forwarding and replies to the January 16, 2022 6:54 PM email from foiacompliance@gmail.com Subject: Chief FOIA Officers Council Meeting February 2, 2022, 1400 EST.
2.	Records of receipt, forwarding and replies to any emails received from FOIA Officers or other party  regarding any January 16, 2022 email from foiacompliance@gmail.com Subject: Chief FOIA Officers Council Meeting February 2, 2022, 1400 EST.
3.	Records of any emails from OGIS or DOJ OIP to Chief FOIA Officers, FOIA professionals or others discussing the right to OGIS dispute resolution, mediation or assistance, FPL dispute resolution or assistance, and/or OGIS or DOJ model language regarding OGIS/FPL assistance, mediation, or dispute resolution services.
4.	I am also seeking a copy of this FOIA Request, which is an Agency record subject to that exists and is in the Agency’s possession at the time of my FOIA request. This record is a responsive record integral to my Request. Release of the Agency’s copy is not optional.

NOTE: To the extent that you contend that any records are exempt, you must identify the specific records and release all segregable portions. I may seek an in-camera inspection in any court proceeding. This is a simple request.

REQUESTED FORMAT. 

I am seeking an ADA accessible PDF file by with: (1) a signed and dated cover letter (citing my personally assigned requester control number); (2) with record page count for all records released records (3) a copy of this request in your reply. I seek records in PDF format with an imbedded copy of my requests to (1) impede the agency from not addressing the FOIA Request; (2) impede the Agency from not providing the documents stated in the Agency’s letter reply, and (3) make it obvious in any subsequent review what the Agency has or has not done. 

Further, I request that these records be sent in any digital formats in which they exist (such as PDF and Excel). Under the terms of the E-FOIA Amendments of 1996, Section 5, if a document exists in electronic format, it must be released in that format upon request.

Each record must be provided as a distinct record in their native format. Emails should be provided as MS Outlook files, if not encrypted or otherwise unable to be open ed by me. Only if this is not possible, emails should be produced with their embedded hyperlinked attachments by using the “File => Save as Adobe PDF” command within Outlook or by other software that produces the same result.

I am also seeking the “Description Available to the Public” field I FOIAonline be set to yes and that all records be released to and viewable in the application by the general Public. The release type must be set to “Unredacted – Releasable to the General Public: Will be available to the general public,” or to “Redacted – Releasable to the General Public: Will be available to the general public.”

This request is distinctly separate from any other. Please do not combine this request with any other request in your reply. I am requesting that each element of the records sought be specifically addressed in the reply.

FEE WAIVER/ PUBLIC INTEREST/PUBLIC RELEASE. Notwithstanding my agreement to pay fees below if my fee waiver is denied, I am seeking a fee waiver due to significant public interest in this information. The subject of the requested records concerns "the operations or activities of the government.” The disclosure is "likely to contribute" to an understanding of government operations or activities. There is no commercial interest. There is significant public interest. I am also seeking the “Description Available to the Public” field I FOIAonline be set to yes and that all records be released to and viewable in the application by the general Public. The release type must be set to “Unredacted – Releasable to the General Public: Will be available to the general public,” or to “Redacted – Releasable to the General Public: Will be available to the general public.”

AGREEMENT TO PAY FEES. 

I agree to pay fees for searching or copying the records up to $25. If the fees exceed this amount please advise me of the cost before proceeding. I do not believe that there should be any charge for providing these records, as there is public interest in government operations. I am a private individual not seeking documents for commercial use, such that the following applies: “No fees may be charged by any DoD Component if the costs of routine collection and processing of the fee are likely to equal or exceed the amount of the fee. With the exception of requesters seeking documents for a commercial use, Components shall provide the first two hours of search time, and the first one hundred pages of duplication without charge.” I would note that because I am requesting an electronic file, there should not be a per page copy fee. The OMB Guidelines direct that searches for responsive records should be done in the "most efficient and least expensive manner." See OMB Fee Guidelines, 52 Fed. Reg. at 10,017. As an “all others” requester, I may only be assessed search and duplication fees and not fees for review. See 32 CFR 286.12 - Schedule of fees. Also, please note that, should payment become necessary, the Coinage Act of 1965, specifically Section 31 U.S.C. 5103, entitled "Legal tender," states: " United States coins and currency (including Federal reserve notes and circulating notes of Federal reserve banks and national banks) are legal tender for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues. Foreign gold or silver coins are not legal tender for debts.
( Pub. L. 97–258, Sept. 13, 1982, 96 Stat. 980 ; Pub. L. 97–452, §1(19), Jan. 12, 1983, 96 Stat. 2477 .)
EXPEDITED PROCESSING. 
I am seeking expedited processing. In any denial of my request for expedited processing the Agency must state in detail how my request does not meet requirement and who, by name, was involved in the denial determination.

The February 2, 2022 stealth Chief FOIA Officers Council meeting was not advertised in the normal way for such meetings and was not posted on either the NARA or DOJ websites (DOJ ma have posted the day before). this meeting was so poorly advertised and not posted in advance to the OGIS or DOJ OIP websites.

2.	There is a reasonable expectation of an imminent loss of a substantial due process rights in connection with statutory times for FOIA actions.
a.	OGIS and DOJ OIP  intentionally did not address my questions submitted in advance of the meeting and during the meeting into the online chat. This appears to be a violation of law affecting my due process rights in connection with open FOIA meetings.

3.	Information is urgently needed to inform the public concerning some actual or alleged government activity/malfeasance. 
a.	See paragraph 1 above.
b.	I am an individual primarily engaged in dissemination of information via extensive email lists, blogs, coordination with Open Government Advocate Organizations and members of the media.

In any denial of my request for expedited processing, I am seeking that the Agency identify who, by name and email was consulted and that the Agency provide specific justification  as to how my request stated herein does not qualify.

STILL-INTERESTED PREEMPTIVE REPLY.  This is a preemptive reply to the Justice Department guidelines the procedure known as a “still interested” inquiry, through which a FOIA officer can confirm that the requester has not lost interest in obtaining the documents.
 
My interest in all FOIA requests submitted to your office is enduring, meaning that my interest in seeking replies to all past and future FOIA request remains in effect until each request has been answered fully and the time for judicial review has passed. Please do not initiate any "still interested" inquiries. This serves as my notice of enduring interest and automatic reply to any future questions of interest by your office. There are no reasonable grounds to ever conclude in the future that I am not interested in this request.

Implementation Checklist for DOJ OIP Guidance on “Still-Interested” Inquiries
1.	Ensure there are reasonable grounds to make a “still-interested” inquiry in first instance.
2.	Absent good cause, do not make multiple “still-interested” inquiries.
3.	Use requester’s preferred method of communication and in the absence of a preference, communicate by telephone or email as the default. 
4.	Memorialize any decision by a requester to withdraw a request that is conveyed by telephone by sending the requester a brief email or letter noting the withdrawal.
5.	Provide requesters no less than thirty (30) working days to respond to the “still-interested” inquiry and ensure that there is a simple way to do so.
6.	Advise the requester that if they elect not to respond to the inquiry, the request will be administratively closed at the conclusion of the designated time period (which must be at least 30 working days).
7.	Prior to administratively closing a request based upon the lack of a response by the requester, make good faith efforts to reach out to the requester using multiple methods of communication.
8.	In the event a requester responds to the “still- interested” inquiry within a reasonable time after the deadline has passed, reopen the request and place it back into the processing queue where it would have been.

PRESERVE RECORDS AND SEARCHES FOR JUDICIAL REVIEW. 

Please search for, locate and preserve all responsive or potentially responsive records and records of your searches in your FOIA case file until the statutory date for judicial review has passed (should that be necessary) or in accordance with a NARA approved records schedule, if longer. NARA GRS 4.2 requires that FOIA and Privacy Act case files be retained for 6 years after final agency action or 3 years after final adjudication by the courts, whichever is later. 
Records of responsive searches would include but not be limited to: searches conducted for each specific record sought and all other records known to the Agency, including dates, manner of searching, responsible agent or employee conducting each search and the results thereof. Such persons determining the locations of responsive records must be inclusive of persons who would know such locations and their identities and manner of determining search locations must be preserved. 

In any subsequent proceedings, I may seek sworn declarations and a court order appointing a special counsel, as appropriate. Similarly, I may pursue additional venues. 

Any deletion of potentially responsive records by any party having knowledge of this Request may be a violation of law. In as much as applicable staff and leadership have knowledge of my subject request, the Agency must search for, locate and preserve all responsive or potentially responsive records and records of searches in their FOIA case file, and leadership must ensure that this is done. Failing to do so and allowing records to be deleted IAW any other records management schedule may be a violation of law.

ELECTRONIC RECORDS PRESERVATION.

The Agency must preserve all electronically stored information, copies and backup, as defined by Rule 34 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, along with any paper files which the Agency maintains, relevant to this action  I am seeking electronic data in the Agency’s custody and control that is relevant to this action, including without limitation emails, along with metadata, and other information contained on Agency computer systems and any electronic storage systems. I consider this electronic data and paper files to be valuable and irreplaceable sources of discoverable information in this matter.  No procedures should have been implemented to alter any active, deleted or fragmented data.  Moreover, no electronic data should have been disposed of or destroyed. (ETL Institute for Advancement of America’s Legal System).  

Further, to properly fulfill your preservation obligation, stop all scheduled data destruction, electronic shredding, rotation of backup tapes, and the sale, gift or destruction of hardware. Notify all individuals and of the need and duty to take the necessary affirmatives steps to comply with the duty to preserve evidence. (2008 Thomson Delmar Learning).

The Agency’s Director of Information Operations or similar organization must initiate procedures to preserve electronic records.

ALTERATION/DESTRUCTION OF RECORDS

Whoever knowingly alters, destroys, mutilates, conceals, covers up, falsifies, or makes a false entry in any record, document, or tangible object with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence the investigation or proper administration of any matter within the jurisdiction of any department or agency of the United States or any case filed under title 11, or in relation to or contemplation of any such matter or case, shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both. 18 U.S. Code § 1519 - Destruction, alteration, or falsification of records. (Added Pub. L. 107–204, title VIII, §802(a), July 30, 2002, 116 Stat. 800.).

18 U.S.C. 641 and 2071. The penalties for the unlawful or accidental removal, defacing, alteration, or destruction of Federal records or the attempt to do so, include a fine, imprisonment, or both (18 U.S.C. 641 and 2071).
36 CFR § 1230 UNLAWFUL OR ACCIDENTAL REMOVAL, DEFACING, ALTERATION, OR DESTRUCTION OF RECORDS
§1230.3   
Unlawful or accidental destruction (also called unauthorized destruction) means disposal of an unscheduled or permanent record; disposal prior to the end of the NARA-approved retention period of a temporary record (other than court-ordered disposal under §1226.14(d) of this subchapter); and disposal of a record subject to a FOIA request, litigation hold, or any other hold requirement to retain the records.
IMPROPOERLY WITHHOLDING RECORDS

Pursuant to FOIA:  
“Whenever the court orders the production of any agency records improperly withheld from the complainant and assesses against the United States reasonable attorney fees and other litigation costs, and the court additionally issues a written finding that the circumstances surrounding the withholding raise questions whether agency personnel acted arbitrarily or capriciously with respect to the withholding, the Special Counsel shall promptly initiate a proceeding to determine whether disciplinary action is warranted against the officer or employee who was primarily responsible for the withholding. The Special Counsel, after investigation and consideration of the evidence submitted, shall submit his findings and recommendations to the administrative authority of the agency concerned and shall send copies of the findings and recommendations to the officer or employee or his representative. The administrative authority shall take the corrective action that the Special Counsel recommends.”  5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i).

PERJURY
Whoever-
(1) having taken an oath before a competent tribunal, officer, or person, in any case in which a law of the United States authorizes an oath to be administered, that he will testify, declare, depose, or certify truly, or that any written testimony, declaration, deposition, or certificate by him subscribed, is true, willfully and contrary to such oath states or subscribes any material matter which he does not believe to be true; or
(2) in any declaration, certificate, verification, or statement under penalty of perjury as permitted under section 1746 of title 28, United States Code, willfully subscribes as true any material matter which he does not believe to be true;
is guilty of perjury and shall, except as otherwise expressly provided by law, be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than five years, or both. This section is applicable whether the statement or subscription is made within or without the United States.
18 U.S. C. § 1621 - Perjury generally (June 25, 1948, ch. 645, 62 Stat. 773; Pub. L. 88–619, §1, Oct. 3, 1964, 78 Stat. 995 ; Pub. L. 94–550, §2, Oct. 18, 1976, 90 Stat. 2534 ; Pub. L. 103–322, title XXXIII, §330016(1)(I), Sept. 13, 1994, 108 Stat. 2147. 
SUBORDINATION OF PERJURY
The term subornation of perjury further describes the circumstance wherein an attorney at law causes a client to lie under oath or allows another party to lie under oath
Title 18 U.S.C. § 1622 provides:
Whoever procures another to commit any perjury is guilty of subornation of perjury, and shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than five years, or both.
FALSE OFFICIAL STATEMENTS.
18 U.S.C. § 1001. Statements or entries generally:
a.	Except as otherwise provided in this section, whoever, in any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch of the Government of the United States, knowingly and willfully --
1.	falsifies, conceals, or covers up by any trick, scheme, or device a material fact;
2.	makes any materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement or representation; or
3.	makes or uses any false writing or document knowing the same to contain any materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement or entry; shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 5 years, or both.
10 U.S. Code § 907. Art. 107. False official statements; false swearing: 
(a) FALSE OFFICIAL STATEMENTS. Any person subject to this chapter who, with intent to deceive— 
(1) signs any false record, return, regulation, order, or other official document, knowing it to be false; or
(2) makes any other false official statement knowing it to be false;

shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.”

LEGAL FRAMEWORK OF FOIA 

1.	The definition of “records” includes:
“[A]ill books, papers, maps, photographs, machine readable materials, or other documentary materials, regardless of physical form or characteristics, made or received by an agency of the United States Government under Federal law or in connection with the transaction of public business and preserved or appropriate for preservation by that agency or its legitimate successor as evidence of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, operations, or other activities of the Government or because of the informational value of data in them.”  44 U.S.C. § 3301 (emphasis supplied).
2.	FOIA requires that “each agency, upon any request for records which (i) reasonably describes such records and (ii) is made in accordance with published rules stating the time, place, fees (if any), and procedures to be followed, shall make the records promptly available to any person” 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(3)(A).
3.	FOIA requires that “each agency shall establish a system to assign an individualized tracking number for each request received that will take longer than ten days to process and provide to each person making a request the tracking number assigned to the request” 5 U.S.C. § 522(a)(7)(A).
4.	FOIA requires that each agency shall “establish a telephone line or Internet service that provides information about the status of a request to the person making the request using the assigned tracking number, including the date on which the agency originally received the request; and an estimated date on which the agency will complete action on the request. 5 U.S.C. § 522(a)(7)(B).
5.	FOIA also requires federal agencies to make a final determination on FOIA administrative appeals that it receives within twenty days (excepting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal public holidays) after the receipt of such appeal, unless the agency expressly provides notice to the requester of “unusual circumstances” meriting additional time for responding to a FOIA request. 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(6)(A)(ii).
6.	FOIA expressly provides that a person shall be deemed to have constructively exhausted their administrative remedies if the agency fails to comply with the applicable time limitations provided by 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(6)(A)(I) - (ii). See also 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(6)(C).
7.	FOIA provides that any person who has not been provided the records requested pursuant to FOIA, after exhausting their administrative remedies, may seek legal redress from the Federal District Court to enjoin the agency from withholding agency records and to order the production of any agency records improperly withheld from the complainant.
8.	Regarding he names of the FOIA requesters, the courts have held hat under the FOIA requesters do not have an expectation of privacy. Stauss v. IRS, 516 F. Supp. 1218, 1223 (D.D.C. 1981),
9.	Under FOIA, the federal agency has the burden of sustaining its actions. 5 U.S.C.§ 552(a)(4)(B).
10.	Pursuant to FOIA, a Court may assess attorney fees and litigation costs against the United States if the Plaintiff prevails in an action thereunder.  5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(E).
11.	Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued a handbook addressing FOIA Annual Reports. See DOJ, Handbook for Agency Annual Freedom of Information Act Reports, “Disposition of FOIA Requests,” (available at http://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/oip/pages/attachments/2014/11/04/department_of_justice_handbook_for_agency_annual_freedom_of_information_act_reports.pdf) (“DOJ Handbook”). 
12.	Among other things, the DOJ Handbook states, “All requests (perfected and non-perfected), appeals, and consultations that were pending at any time during the relevant fiscal year [October 1st through September 30th] will be captured.” 
13.	The DOJ Handbook also states: 
“[E]ach agency is ultimately responsible for the accuracy and completeness of its Annual FOIA Report.  It is therefore essential for agencies to take steps that will ensure that they are adequately tracking all of the information necessary to complete the Annual FOIA Report sections detailed below. Agencies that utilize a tracking or case management system for this purpose are responsible for ensuring that the system they are using can produce an accurate Annual FOIA Report that is in compliance with the law and Department of Justice guidance.” DOJ Handbook, at 3.

communications.subject: FOIA Expedited Processing Disposition Reached for NARA-NGC-2022-000788
communications.communication:
Your request for Expedited Processing for the FOIA request NARA-NGC-2022-000788 has been 
			denied. 
		Additional details for this request are as follows: 
 
  * Request Created on:
					02/18/2022 
  * Request Description:
					Please See attachment for description. 
  * Expedited Processing Original Justification:
					I am seeking expedited processing. In any denial of my request for expedited processing the Agency must state in detail how my request does not meet requirement and who, by name, was involved in the denial determination. 
1. The subject is of widespread and exceptional media interest and the information sought involves possible questions about the government's integrity that affect public confidence. 
a. U.S.C § 552(k)(6)(B) requires the full Council, not just the co-chairs. Did OGIS announce the meeting as the full Council and notify all in the same manner as other Council meetings Per FOIA. “Not less frequently than annually, the Council shall hold a meeting that shall be open to the public and permit interested persons to appear and present oral and written statements to the Council.” This meeting did not meet those requirements. 
b. There was no such a meeting per 5 USC § 552(k)(6)(B) in 202, 2020, 2019, etc. 
c. The February 2, 2022 stealth Chief FOIA Officers Council meeting was not advertised in the normal way for such meetings and was not posted on either the NARA or DOJ websites (DOJ ma have posted the day before). this meeting was so poorly advertised and not posted in advance to the OGIS or DOJ OIP websites. 
d. The meeting was not on You Tube for public viewing and preservation. I have not seen that before for a FOIA open meeting. 
e. Federal Register Notice 01/20/2022 says, “Additional details about the Chief FOIA Officers Council and the meeting, including the agenda, are available on OGIS's website.” This was false. 
f. Chief FOIA Officer and FOIA Advisory Committee meetings are typically 3 hours not 1 hour. 
g. Comments were limited to 5 min per requester. 
h. I have been in contact with multiple members of the media regarding these matters, both before and after the meeting, There is exceptional interest in Saving FOIA Part II. 
i. OGIS and DOJ OIP intentionally did not address my questions submitted in advance of the meeting and during the meeting into the online chat. This appears to be a violation of law. 
j. DOJ and NARA continue to hold unlawful meetings. FOIA Improvement Act states, “Not later than 10 business days before a meeting of the Council, notice of such meeting shall be published in the Federal Register.” Not done for the Nov17, 2021 meeting. ?OGIS: For Nov17, 2021 meeting oral comments were limited to 3 minutes, even though 15 minutes were allocated and I continued to call in. Why the limitation and why was I not recognized a 2nd time? 

2. There is a reasonable expectation of an imminent loss of a substantial due process rights in connection with statutory times for FOIA actions. 
a. OGIS and DOJ OIP intentionally did not address my questions submitted in advance of the meeting and during the meeting into the online chat. This appears to be a violation of law affecting my due process rights in connection with open FOIA meetings. 

3. Information is urgently needed to inform the public concerning some actual or alleged government activity/malfeasance. 
a. See paragraph 1 above. 
b. I am an individual primarily engaged in dissemination of information via extensive email lists, blogs, coordination with Open Government Advocate Organizations and members of the media. 

In any denial of my request for expedited processing, I am seeking that the Agency identify who, by name and email was consulted and that the Agency provide specific justification as to how my request stated herein does not qualify. 

STILL-INTERESTED PREEMPTIVE REPLY. This is a preemptive reply to the Justice Department guidelines the procedure known as a “still interested” inquiry, through which a FOIA officer can confirm that the requester has not lost interest in obtaining the documents. 
  * Expedited Processing Disposition Reason:
					After carefully reviewing your request, we do not believe expedition is warranted, as you have not demonstrated that your request meets the above-referenced criteria.  Specifically, you have not provided evidence that there is an urgent need to inform the public of a government activity, or widespread and exceptional media interest involving questions affecting public confidence in the Government’s integrity that can be addressed by the records you seek.  You also have not provided evidence that there is a reasonable expectation of any imminent loss of a substantial due process rights in connection with the statutory times of FOIA actions with the records you seek.  If you are not satisfied with our action on your request for expedited processing, you have the right to file an administrative appeal in writing by mail or email.  If by mail, please address your appeal to the Deputy Archivist (N), National Archives and Records Administration, 8601 Adelphi Rd., College Park, Maryland 20740. Both the letter and the envelope should be clearly marked “Freedom of Information Act Appeal.” If by email, please submit your appeal to FOIA@nara.gov addressed to the Deputy Archivist.  Your appeal should be received within 90 calendar days of the date of this denial, and it should explain why you think this response does not meet the requirements of the FOIA. 
If you would like to discuss our response before filing an appeal to attempt to resolve your dispute without going through the appeals process, you may contact our FOIA Public Liaison Gary M. Stern for assistance via email at garym.stern@nara.gov. 
You may also contact the Office of Government Information Services (OGIS), the Federal FOIA Ombudsman’s office, which offers mediation services to help resolve disputes between FOIA requesters and Federal agencies. The contact information for OGIS is noted below: 
Email:  ogis@nara.gov  Website:  ogis.archives.gov 
Tel:  202-741-5770 or 1-877-684-6448

communications.communication:
NARA's responses have nothing whatsoever to do with the records I am seeking. 
Therefore, I am seeking FPL dispute resolution from Gary Stern to this FOIA request.
RECORDS SOUGHT VIA FOIA.

NARA 22-U.R.MUCK. OGIS ADR +Chief FOIA Officers Meeting 2 Feb 2022
See PDF. See Requested Format.

Background.

1. By emails from foiacompliance@gmail.com of January 16, 2022, Subject: Chief FOIA Officers Council Meeting February 2, 2022, 1400 EST, I notified several hundred Chief FOIA Officers and FOIA Professionals of said meeting and further stated:

Please pay particular attention to the attached Public Comment, “Mandatory Right to OGIS Dispute Resolution (20220116).” Your agency is likely citing unlawful language, potentially as the result of previously disseminated errant OGIS guidance as OGIS may have sought to minimize workload due to grossly inadequate funding for mediation (and FOIA compliance oversight).

2. On January 16, 2022 6:54 PM I nest that same email (Attachment A) to ogisopenmeeting@nara.gov; alina.semo@nara.gov; bobak.Talebian@usdoj.gov; kirsten.mitchell@nara.gov; Vanita.Gupta19@usdoj.gov; debra.wall@nara.gov; martha.murphy@nara.gov; sheela.portonovo@nara.gov; carrie.mcguire@nara.gov; teresa.brady@nara.gov; dwaine.bacon@nara.gov; jessica.hartman@nara.gov; christa.lemelin@nara.gov; garym.stern@nara.gov.

3. OGIS Director, recently stated (contrary to law and OGIS/DOJ model language policy), “Agencies have the option to include either or both the FPL and OGIS in adverse determinations.”

4. NARA, DOJ, and agencies across the Federal Government have been citing unlawful language wrt OGIS dispute resolution requiring requesters to contact the Agency FPL first:

“If you are unable to resolve your FOIA dispute through our FOIA Public Liaison, the Office of Government Information Services (OGIS), the Federal FOIA Ombudsman’s office, offers mediation services to help resolve disputes between FOIA requesters and Federal agencies.”

Requested Records.

I am respectfully seeking as individual files records in NARA’s custody only from January 15 2022 to present records related to said January 16, 2022 emails and any emails or other OGIS or DOJ correspondence relating to OGIS dispute resolution services as follows:

1. Records of receipt, forwarding and replies to the January 16, 2022 6:54 PM email from foiacompliance@gmail.com Subject: Chief FOIA Officers Council Meeting February 2, 2022, 1400 EST.
2. Records of receipt, forwarding and replies to any emails received from FOIA Officers or other party regarding any January 16, 2022 email from foiacompliance@gmail.com Subject: Chief FOIA Officers Council Meeting February 2, 2022, 1400 EST.
3. Records of any emails from OGIS or DOJ OIP to Chief FOIA Officers, FOIA professionals or others discussing the right to OGIS dispute resolution, mediation or assistance, FPL dispute resolution or assistance, and/or OGIS or DOJ model language regarding OGIS/FPL assistance, mediation, or dispute resolution services.
4. I am also seeking a copy of this FOIA Request, which is an Agency record subject to that exists and is in the Agency’s possession at the time of my FOIA request. This record is a responsive record integral to my Request. Release of the Agency’s copy is not optional.

NOTE: To the extent that you contend that any records are exempt, you must identify the specific records and release all segregable portions. I may seek an in-camera inspection in any court proceeding. This is a simple request.

title: Police PROTECT Act Compliance Sept-Oct 2026 (Norwood Police Department)

communications.subject: Massachusetts Public Records Law Request: Police PROTECT Act Compliance Sept-Oct 2026 (Norwood Police Department)
communications.communication:
Dear Record Access Officer:

This is a request under the Massachusetts Public Records Law (M. G. L. Chapter 66, Section 10). I am requesting the following records:

1.    All municipal or police department policies, ordinances, or resolutions currently in effect regarding communication and information sharing between departmental employees and federal agents/agencies within the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) or the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including but not limited to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The records request includes, but is not limited to, policies regarding:

             A. Fingerprint and other data sharing;
             B. Compliance with federal immigration enforcement efforts, including guidance or policies concerning when communication with ICE officers is allowed. This includes how and under what circumstances to respond to ICE detainer requests or when and how department employees can provide a federal immigration authority with nonpublic personal information, custody status, or advance notice of a person’s release from pretrial detention or upcoming court appearances;
             C. Any other records that indicate changes in policy or practice as a result of the passage of the Massachusetts PROTECT Act in August 2026.

 2.  All departmental and municipal policies, guidance, memos or other records concerning the use of local resources for federal civil immigration enforcement. This includes policies, requests or responses to requests for the use of municipal parking lots, police station interior or exterior areas for immigration enforcement, staging, or the transfer of custody.

3.    Any records of email, text, or phone conversations between department employees and federal DHS employees working at ICE made from September 4, 2026 until October 31, 2026 (or the date responsive records are collected for review if prior to October 31, 2026), including but not limited to email sent to any “@ice.dhs.gov” email address. This request includes any call logs or transcripts of calls.

For each request, I am not seeking identifying information of community members, and I will accept anonymized or redacted data as necessary to protect the identity of the public. Redaction of names of municipal, state, or federal government employees is not necessary.

Pursuant to 950 CMR 32.07(2)(k), I request that your agency waive fees given that these records are in the public interest and I am not requesting this for commercial interests. In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. The Public Records Law requires a written response within 10 business days. If you cannot comply with my request, you are statutorily required to provide an explanation in writing.

Sincerely,

Joshua Dankoff
Director of Strategic Initaitives
Citizens for Juvenile Justice
joshuadankoff@cfjj.org
(submitted via muckrock)

with the FBI, DHS and ICE on immigration matters.  We do follow state
issued guidelines and policies.  When a subject is arrested and
fingerprinted, their prints are sent to the previously mentioned agencies
under the Secure Communities Act.  We DO NOT contact DHS or ICE regarding
immigration matters.  In these cases the person arrested is sent to court
after processing.  I've attached an email sent to all personnel on
September 9, 2026, regarding the Massachusetts Protect Act.  (Question C.)

Federal Agencies are not allowed to use our parking lot for law enforcement
issues involving only immigration matters.  We do not have a role with DHS
or ICE in the field unless a criminal issue develops while they are
performing their duties.  Lastly, I checked with our Detective Division
personnel in regards to any contact with DHS or ICe personnel between
September 4, 2026 and October 31, 2026.  There was no contact during this
time period.

Respectfully,
Officer Kevin Riley

title: Initial-contract (CBM) cases and their outcomes, October 1999 to present

communications.subject: Freedom of Information Act Request: Initial-contract (CBM) cases and their outcomes, October 1999 to present
communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, I hereby request the following records:

Please include all cases with N-Category "Initial Contract" (Case Type CBM) opened or received from October 1, 1999 through the date the search is run, whatever the case's status or reason for closing. That means cases closed with "Agreement Reached" and also, for example:

- "Parties Failed to Respond"
- "Case Cancelled"
- "Question re: Representation"
- "Employees Included In/Folded Into Existing Unit"
- "Facility Closed"
- "Other"
- cases with no reason for closing recorded
- cases still open

My earlier request FOIA-2022-00042 was fulfilled with only cases closed as "Agreement Reached".

For this request I am asking that cases which did not reach agreement can be counted.

Fields. For each case, please provide the following, where they exist. Field names are from the extract produced for FOIA-2022-00042:
1. The FMCS case number or other unique case identifier
2. Received Date; Initiated Date; the date the case was closed
3. Case Type; N-Case Type; N-Category; N-Case Source (for example F-7 from Union, F-7 from Organization, NLRB, FLRA)
4. N-Date Submitted, and any identifier linking the case to its F-7 notice
5. The NLRB case number (for example 13-RC-123456), or the certification date, for cases opened from NLRB certifications
6. Basis for Closing (Case Statistics)
7. Contract Agreement Date
8. Employer; Union; Union Local; bargaining unit size (BU)
9. The employer's location and the affected or bargaining-unit location (city, state, ZIP code)
10. The industry code (NAICS), if recorded
11. Whether a mediator held joint or separate meetings, and the number and dates of those meetings, if recorded

Personal information. To make processing easier, you may leave out the names, telephone numbers and email addresses of individual employer and union contacts. I do not need them. Please do not leave out the employer or union names.

Older records. If cases from before a particular year are in a legacy system, or have fewer fields, please provide whatever is available for those years, and tell me which fields or years are missing rather than withholding the rest.

Format. I would like the records as a spreadsheet or delimited text file (.xlsx or .csv), one row per case, in the form the system exports. If producing all years would take much longer, please send each portion as it becomes ready, starting with the most recent years.

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 20 business days, as the statute requires.

Sincerely,

Forest Gregg

communications.subject: RE: Freedom of Information Act Request #FOIA-2027-00003
communications.communication:
Thank you for your letter. 

I request a waiver of all fees. If the waiver is denied, I agree to pay fees up to $100, and I ask that you contact me before incurring anything higher. I am not a commercial requester. I ask to be placed in the "all other requesters" fee category, which includes two hours of search time and 100 pages (or the electronic equivalent) at no charge. Because I am asking for an electronic export of existing records, I expect duplication costs to be minimal.

Fee waiver request

Disclosure is in the public interest because it is likely to contribute significantly to public understanding of the operations or activities of the government, and it is not primarily in my commercial interest. 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(A)(iii).

1. The records concern identifiable operations of the government. The records document one specific FMCS program. Under 29 U.S.C. § 173 and Section 8(d) of the National Labor Relations Act, FMCS offers mediation to parties bargaining a first contract. Since about 2003, it has opened those cases partly from certifications the NLRB sends it. The records show:
- which newly certified units FMCS opened cases for;
- how long the cases lasted;
- how each case was closed: agreement reached, parties failed to respond, facility closed, or otherwise.

These are FMCS's own records of how it carries out a statutory duty.

2. The records are meaningfully informative and not already public. FMCS publishes F-7 notice data, but it does not publish the outcomes of its initial-contract cases. My earlier request, FOIA-2022-00042, produced only the cases closed as "Agreement Reached". The public therefore sees FMCS's successes but not its full caseload.

The only published study using comparable FMCS case records covers 1999–2004 (Ferguson, Industrial and Labor Relations Review, 2008), and those records are not public. Using the public F-7 and NLRB data alone, I have found that only about a third of units newly certified since 1999 later show a renewed contract. Public data cannot show whether the rest never reached a first contract, reached one and lost it, or never had an FMCS case at all. The requested records answer that question directly.

Policy researchers have pointed to this gap. A 2026 Economic Policy Institute report observes that the role of employer-side law firms in "frustrating workers' attempts to reach a first contract has largely gone unexamined" (Poydock, Wiggin and McNicholas 2026). FMCS's case records are the only systematic federal record of what happens in first-contract bargaining.

3. Disclosure will reach a reasonably broad audience, and I have the ability and expertise to deliver it. Since 2021, I have maintained labordata (https://labordata.bunkum.us/), a free public warehouse of 15 federal labor datasets. It includes NLRB case and election records, FMCS F-7 notices and work-stoppage data, voluntary recognitions, OSHA and Wage and Hour enforcement records, and Department of Labor union and employer disclosure filings. It needs no login, and offers a web interface, an API, CSV export and direct database queries.

It is heavily used. Over the most recent three months, labordata answered roughly 48,000 data queries, after excluding automated crawlers, from more than 300 distinct client applications. It also receives a few thousand browser visits a month. Its users include:
- university researchers;
- a labor-watchdog nonprofit that queries it daily;
- union researchers
- labor-relations consultants;

In a single recent week, users connected from the networks of at least seven universities, including UCLA, NYU and Penn State.

Researchers and policy organizations rely on it:
- Pezold, Jäger and Nüss, "Labor Market Tightness and Union Activity" (NBER Working Paper 31988, 2023), measures strikes using the FMCS work-stoppage data I collected and published.
- The Economic Policy Institute's 2026 report on employer spending on union avoidance, which examines the firms involved in "the stalling of first contract negotiations", uses NLRB data from labordata and cites it as a source (Poydock, Wiggin and McNicholas 2026).

I will release these records on labordata, free of charge and with documentation, joined to NLRB election records so that each case can be traced to the certification that started it. I will also publish an analysis of first-contract outcomes by year, industry and region.

Linking FMCS case records to NLRB certifications takes specialized knowledge of both agencies' data. I have already built that linkage for the F-7 notices, so the public will get usable information rather than a raw extract.

4. The contribution to public understanding will be significant. No public source today says how often FMCS's first-contract cases end in agreement, or how many newly certified units FMCS reaches at all. Timely first contracts are a matter of active national policy debate. The PRO Act, for example, would establish "a bargaining process for reaching a first contract in a timely manner", with FMCS mediation and arbitration (Poydock, Wiggin and McNicholas 2026). Evaluating such proposals requires knowing how FMCS's existing first-contract program performs. These records would provide the first public measure of that in two decades.

5. The request is not primarily in my commercial interest. I have no commercial interest in these records. labordata is noncommercial, and everything it publishes is free.

If FMCS grants only part of the waiver, I ask for a waiver of whatever portion of the fees qualifies. If the waiver is denied, I agree to pay fees up to $100, and I ask that you contact me before incurring anything higher.

Sincerely,
Forest Gregg

title: Oklahoma County District Attorney Office Concerning OCPD Forensic Analyst Elaine Taylor Crime Lab Records

communications.subject: Oklahoma Open Records Act Request: Oklahoma County District Attorney Office Concerning OCPD Forensic Analyst Elaine Taylor Crime Lab Records
communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the Oklahoma Open Records Act, I hereby request the following records:

To whom it may concern:

Pursuant to the Oklahoma Open Records Act, 51 O.S. §§ 24A.1 et seq., I hereby request access to and copies of records in the possession, custody, or control of the Oklahoma County District Attorney’s office concerning Elaine Taylor, a former forensic analyst with the Oklahoma City Police Department crime lab. This request includes crime lab records of a high-profile, controversial former government employee who has publicly admitted she destroyed forensic evidence and whose work is clearly in the public interest.

The Open Records Act is to be liberally construed in favor of disclosure, and any claimed exemption must be narrowly applied and strictly justified. 

Title 51, Section 24A.7 (A) states that a "public body may keep personnel records confidential." (Emphasis added.) This provision does not mandate confidentiality of personnel records; the word “may” connotes discretion. (Mott v. Carlson, 1990 OK 10, 16 & n.4, 786 P.2d 1247, 1249 & n.4; Falconhead Prop. Owners Ass'n v. Fredrickson, 2002 ΟΚ CIV APP 67, 15, 50 P.3d 224, 226, Ross v. City of Owasso, 2017 OK CIV App 4, 389 P.3d 396, 400.) 

Open records exemptions covered by Subsection A (1) and Subsection A(2) do not apply here. This request does not seek private information such as home addresses, telephone numbers, and social security numbers of past or current employees. § 24A.7(D). This request does not seek records pertaining to a current employee. Ms. Taylor retired in February 2017. 

The request seeks public records regardless of format (paper, electronic, email, database entries, audit logs, attachments, or metadata) and covers the entirety of Ms. Taylor’s employment with OCPD, including any records in the possession of the District Attorney’s Office, created before, during, and after her active employment, whether maintained by the Crime Laboratory, Internal Affairs, Professional Standards, Human Resources, or any supervisory or administrative unit. 

This request includes any and all records shared with any other outside entities pertaining to Ms. Taylor’s credibility, reliability, discipline, errors, misconduct, and forensic integrity.

These records include, but are not limited to:

Employment applications, resumes, hiring documents, and job descriptions

Dates of employment, assignments, promotions, demotions, or transfers

Performance evaluations, reviews, or appraisals

Training records, certifications, continuing education, and proficiency testing

Commendations, awards, or letters of recognition

Internal Affairs investigations, Professional Standards reviews, or administrative inquiries

Citizen complaints, prosecutorial complaints, judicial findings, or defense challenges

Disciplinary actions, counseling memoranda, reprimands, suspensions, or terminations

Findings of misconduct, negligence, error, or policy violations

Any investigations, whether formal or informal, that were sustained, not sustained, unfounded, or administratively closed
Retirement, resignation, or separation from employment

Exit interviews or separation memoranda

Post-employment restrictions, consulting agreements, or testimony disclosures
Any and all e-mails pertaining to the above listed items

In addition, this request covers all records reflecting issues related to forensic reliability or compliance, including:
Errors, mistakes, corrective actions, or remediation involving forensic testing or reporting

Nonconformities, deviations, or quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) issues

Testimony reviews, peer review critiques, technical review comments, or supervisory concerns

Corrective action reports, root-cause analyses, or retraining documentation

Any and all e-mails pertaining to the above listed items

These records also include Accreditation, Audit, and External Review Materials and other materials reflecting:

ASCLD/LAB, ANAB, or other accreditation audits referencing Elaine Taylor

External audits, inspections, or compliance reviews

Correspondence with accrediting bodies, prosecutors, or oversight agencies

Findings, warnings, or recommendations related to her work

Case reviews, retesting decisions, or post-conviction inquiries involving her forensic work

Notifications to prosecutors regarding credibility, reliability, or disclosure concerns

Brady, Giglio, or impeachment-related determinations or disclosures

Any and all e-mails pertaining to the above listed items, including any and all communications with District Attorneys, defense counsel, and courts concerning her work
If any portion of this request is denied or redacted, identify the specific statutory exemption relied upon, as required by 51 O.S. § 24A.5(4).

Please do not withhold entire documents where partial redaction is possible. Please ensure that all email, audit logs, and electronic systems are searched for responsive documents.

If records are maintained electronically, I request production in native electronic format where possible.

If the scope of this request can be narrowed to reduce cost or burden, please contact me before denying any portion of the request.
Please advise in advance of any copying or production costs exceeding $25.00. If fees are assessed, provide an itemized estimate pursuant to Oklahoma law.

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 10 business days.

Sincerely,

Jennifer Holtzclaw

communications.subject: RE: Oklahoma Open Records Act Request: Oklahoma County District Attorney Office Concerning OCPD Forensic Analyst Elaine Taylor Crime Lab Records
communications.communication:
Lisa Erickson Endres, Assistant District Attorney 
Oklahoma County District Attorney's Office 
211 N. Robinson Ave., Ste. N700 
Oklahoma City, OK 73102 

October 2, 2026

Via MuckRock (Request No. 199925) and email to Lisa.Endres@oklahomacounty.org

Re: Open Records Act request submitted December 15, 2025, concerning former OCPD Forensic Analyst Elaine Taylor, and the Office's denial letter dated September 18, 2026

Dear Ms. Endres:
I write in response to your letter of September 18, 2026, denying my December 15, 2025, request under the Oklahoma Open Records Act, 51 O.S. §§ 24A.1 et seq. I ask the Office to withdraw the denial, search for responsive records, and produce them or identify the specific statutory exemption applied to each record withheld.
The Office's own Exhibit ORR 1 shows my request went unanswered for 277 days because it was filed away and never forwarded for processing. The grounds stated in the denial do not support withholding every responsive record without a search.
The 277-Day Delay
A public body "must provide prompt, reasonable access to its records." 51 O.S. § 24A.5(6). Any delay "shall be limited solely to the time required for preparing the requested documents and the avoidance of excessive disruptions of the public body's essential functions." Id.
I submitted the request through MuckRock to OCDA@oklahomacounty.org on December 15, 2025. MuckRock sent follow-up requests for a response on my behalf to the same address on December 30, 2025, and on January 14, January 29, February 13, March 2, March 17, April 1, April 16, May 1, May 18, June 2, June 17, July 2, July 17, August 3, August 18, September 2, and September 17, 2026. The Office did not acknowledge the request or any follow-up, ask for clarification, or respond in any form until September 18, 2026, 277 days after submission and one day after the final follow-up.
The Office's own exhibit explains the delay. At 11:34 a.m. on September 17, 2026, Brook Arbeitman forwarded the request to you with the note that it "was filed away and not forwarded at the time." The same email noted that "Jennifer Holtzclaw is involved." (Ex. ORR 1.) The Act opens public records "to any person," 51 O.S. § 24A.5, and conditions access on no showing about who the requester is.
No documents were prepared during those 277 days, and the denial letter claims no disruption of the Office's functions. The Office issued the denial the day after the request was located, on grounds that required no search. Section 24A.5(6) allows delay only to prepare the records or to avoid disrupting the Office's work. Leaving the request in a file served neither purpose.
The Act "fixes a mandatory duty" on public officials to provide prompt, reasonable access. Branstetter v. Fallin, No. CV-2014-2372, Journal Entry of Judgment at 4 (Okla. Cnty. Dist. Ct. May 15, 2018). In Branstetter, the Department of Public Safety produced its first records about 11 months after the request and its first emails about 24 months after, and the Governor's office produced its first records about 17 months after. Id. at 3. Neither request had been formally denied. Id. The court entered declaratory judgment that both officials violated the Act by failing to provide prompt and reasonable access, and held that neither the delays "nor the process which resulted in the delays" was prompt or reasonable. Id. at 4.
The Oklahoma Supreme Court has described the Legislature's "emphatic message to government agencies" that, unless records are specifically excluded, "the public must have prompt and reasonable access to records." Okla. Ass'n of Broadcasters, Inc. v. City of Norman, 2016 OK 119, ¶ 15, 390 P.3d 689. The Office produced nothing for 277 days and then denied the request in full.
The Attorney General has advised that a district attorney "has no authority to withhold public records from inspection and copying" and that prompt, reasonable access "generally may include only the time required to locate and compile such public records." 1999 OK AG 58, ¶ 15(2); see id. ¶ 11.
The Stated Grounds for Denial
Ms. Taylor's employer
The letter states that Ms. Taylor was never an employee of the Office, so the Office holds no personnel records about her. The request did not ask for an Office personnel file. It asked for records "in the possession, custody, or control of the Oklahoma County District Attorney's office concerning Elaine Taylor." It named Brady, Giglio, and impeachment determinations, notifications to prosecutors about her credibility or reliability, and communications with district attorneys, defense counsel, and courts concerning her work.
A record under the Act includes any document "created by, received by, under the authority of, or coming into the custody, control or possession of public officials, public bodies, or their representatives." 51 O.S. § 24A.3(1). Records the Office received from OCPD, and records the Office itself created about Ms. Taylor's work and its own disclosure duties, are records of the Office whoever employed her. The request covers any record showing whether and when the Office received records concerning Ms. Taylor from OCPD, including transmittal letters, cover emails, and receipt logs. If the Office holds no such records, I request that you say so.
Identifiable information and time frame
The letter states that the request lacks identifiable information and a time frame. Since November 1, 2025, before this request was submitted, § 24A.5(7) has defined reasonable specificity as a general time frame, identifiable records, and search terms specific enough to help the public body find them. When a request falls short, the public body "may ask the requestor to clarify the request." 51 O.S. § 24A.5(7). Denial for lack of specificity is permitted only after the public body "has engaged with the requestor to seek the information needed to fulfill the request and to identify the records sought." Id.
The Office did not engage. The request asked the Office to "contact me before denying any portion of the request." The Office denied it without contact.
The request also meets each element. It set its time frame as the whole of Ms. Taylor's OCPD employment, including records created before, during, and after it, and stated that she retired in February 2017. It named specific categories of records. It supplied the search term the Office needs, Ms. Taylor's name, with her title and agency.
The letter states that the Office files criminal cases by defendant name, case number, and police incident number. That explanation covers case files. It does not cover email, correspondence with OCPD, Brady and Giglio determinations, or communications with defense counsel and courts, which the request named and which can be searched by Ms. Taylor's name. Section 24A.5(6) allows procedures that protect the organization of records, and it gives a filing system no power to exempt records from the Act. For case files, the relevant case is State v. Holtzclaw, Oklahoma County No. CF-2014-5869, Court of Criminal Appeals No. F-2016-62.
The letter cites 19 O.S. § 215.22 and states that felony files may be destroyed ten years after the last action. The letter does not state that any responsive record has been destroyed. CF-2014-5869 has had appellate and post-conviction activity since judgment, so no ten-year period has run in that case. Ms. Taylor retired in February 2017, and records about her created since then are less than ten years old under any reading of the schedule. If any responsive record has been destroyed, I ask the Office to identify it, the date of destruction, and the authority relied on.
Availability through the court clerk
The letter suggests that responsive material may be found on OSCN or through the Court Clerk. The 2017 filings concerning Ms. Taylor in F-2016-62 were filed under seal and remain sealed under the Court of Criminal Appeals orders of June 8, 2018, and June 14, 2018. They are not available on OSCN. The Office's email, correspondence, and disclosure records were never filed in any court.
The "original source" exemption
The letter cites "51 O.S. §24A.A" for an exemption covering information available from other law enforcement agencies. The Act contains no section by that number. The closest provision is the second sentence of § 24A.20, which allows a law enforcement agency to "deny access to a copy of such a record in an investigative file if the record or a true and complete copy thereof is available for public inspection and copying at another public body." 51 O.S. § 24A.20. That sentence applies only when the same record is open for public inspection and copying somewhere else. The letter identifies no responsive record that OCPD makes available to the public. The 2017 materials concerning Ms. Taylor remain sealed "unless and until" released by the City of Oklahoma City. Holtzclaw v. State, No. F-2016-62, Order Denying Motion to Unseal Proceedings at 1-2 (Okla. Crim. App. June 14, 2018). If the Office relies on a different provision, I ask it to identify the section by number.
A referral to OCPD also leaves the Office's own records unaddressed. Brady and Giglio determinations made by the Office, its correspondence with OCPD, and its communications with defense counsel and courts originated with the Office.

Section 24A.12
Section 24A.12 provides that the district attorney "may keep its litigation files and investigatory reports confidential." The word "may" makes the provision permissive and discretionary. See Mott v. Carlson, 1990 OK 10, ¶ 6 & n.4, 786 P.2d 1247, 1249 & n.4; Falconhead Prop. Owners Ass'n v. Fredrickson, 2002 OK CIV APP 67, ¶ 5, 50 P.3d 224, 226. Exceptions to disclosure are read narrowly in light of the Act's purpose, which is to "ensure and facilitate the public's right of access to and review of government records." 51 O.S. § 24A.2. 
The Attorney General reads § 24A.12 the same way: confidentiality of a district attorney's litigation files "is within the discretion of the office involved." 1999 OK AG 58, ¶ 8.
The Supreme Court construes the Act "to allow access unless an exception clearly applies," and "the burden is on the public agency seeking to deny access to show a record should not be made available." Broadcasters, 2016 OK 119, ¶ 15 (citing Citizens Against Taxpayer Abuse, Inc. v. City of Oklahoma City, 2003 OK 65, ¶ 12, 73 P.3d 871, 875). A district attorney's office was a defendant in Broadcasters, and the Court ordered the requested record produced. Id. ¶¶ 23, 31.
A discretionary exemption requires an actual decision by the public body about the records at issue, and that decision is reviewable for abuse of discretion. Ross v. City of Owasso, 2017 OK CIV APP 4, ¶¶ 10-11, 18, 389 P.3d 396, 399-401. In Ross, the court could not review the city's withholding because the city had never decided whether to release the report, and it remanded for a proper response to the request. Id. ¶ 18.
The letter states that the Office "does not elect to disclose any of its investigative files" and that the requested records, "if received, would be part of the District Attorney's investigative file." The Office has not searched for, identified, or reviewed any responsive record. A blanket election over records the Office has not located is no exercise of discretion over them. I ask for a record-by-record determination.
Placing a record in a file does not make it confidential. "Access to records which, under the Oklahoma Open Records Act, would otherwise be available for public inspection and copying, shall not be denied because a public body or public official is using or has taken possession of such records for investigatory purposes or has placed the records in a litigation or investigation file." 51 O.S. § 24A.20. Records the Office received from other public bodies keep whatever status they had when they arrived.
Section 24A.12 covers "litigation files and investigatory reports." Email about an analyst's reliability, Brady and Giglio determinations that apply to an analyst across many cases, and communications with accrediting bodies or oversight agencies are records of a different kind. If the Office places any of them within the litigation file of a particular case, I ask it to identify the case.
Impeachment information the Office has already disclosed to defense counsel or courts in any case has left the Office's control. The Act contains no provision allowing a public body to release a record to some members of the public and withhold it from others.
Finally, "[a]ny reasonably segregable portion of a record containing exempt material shall be provided after deletion of the exempt portions." 51 O.S. § 24A.5(3). The request asked the Office to redact rather than withhold whole documents. The denial withheld everything.
Priority Categories and Search Terms
To speed the search, I identify the following categories for first production. This identification does not narrow or waive the remainder of the December 15, 2025, request.
1.	Brady, Giglio, or impeachment determinations, disclosure lists, notices, or memoranda concerning Elaine Taylor, January 1, 2014, to the present.
2.	Email and correspondence between the Office and OCPD, including the OCPD Crime Laboratory and the Municipal Counselor's Office, concerning Ms. Taylor's work, testimony, quality reviews, discipline, suspension, or retirement, January 1, 2016, to the present.
3.	Communications from the Office to defense counsel or to any court disclosing impeachment information about Ms. Taylor, in any case, January 1, 2014, to the present.
4.	Records in the Office's file for State v. Holtzclaw, CF-2014-5869, received from OCPD at any time concerning any review of Ms. Taylor's work or testimony.

Suggested search terms for email and electronic files are "Elaine Taylor," "E. Taylor," "Taylor" within the same message as "lab" or "DNA," "Brady," "Giglio," and "crime lab."
I will pay copying costs as permitted by § 24A.5(4). No search fee may be charged "when the release of records is in the public interest," including release to taxpayers "seeking to determine whether those entrusted with the affairs of the government are honestly, faithfully, and competently performing their duties as public servants." 51 O.S. § 24A.5(4).
Requested Action
I ask the Office to take the following steps by October 14, 2026.
1.	Withdraw the September 18, 2026, denial and search for records responsive to the request, beginning with the priority categories above.
2.	Produce responsive records, or for each record withheld, identify the specific statutory exemption by section number.
3.	Produce every reasonably segregable portion of any record withheld in part, as § 24A.5(3) requires.
4.	Preserve all responsive records, including any eligible for destruction under 19 O.S. § 215.22, until this request is resolved.
If the Office has not withdrawn the denial by that date, I intend to seek review through the Public Access Counselor under 51 O.S. § 24A.40(B) and (D) and to consider an action under 51 O.S. § 24A.17. 

Sincerely,

Jennifer Holtzclaw 

MuckRock News, DEPT MR 199925 263 Huntington Ave. Boston, MA 02115 199925-35053988@requests.muckrock.com

communications.communication:
To the Oklahoma County District Attorney’s Office:

I am writing to follow up on my appeal of the denial of my Oklahoma Open Records Act request concerning former Oklahoma City Police Department forensic analyst Elaine Taylor and related crime laboratory records.

As of October 26, 2026, 18 business days have elapsed since my appeal was submitted on October 1, 2026, without a response or acknowledgment from your office.

Under the Oklahoma Open Records Act, 51 O.S. § 24A.5, public bodies are required to provide prompt, reasonable access to public records. Although the statute does not prescribe a specific number of days for responding to an appeal, the requirement of promptness and reasonableness remains applicable to an agency’s handling of requests for access to public records.

The Oklahoma Attorney General’s guidance further explains that delays in providing access must be reasonably related to the time necessary to prepare responsive records or avoid excessive disruption of an agency’s essential functions.

My appeal challenges an existing denial and requests reconsideration of the statutory grounds for withholding the identified records. At this stage, I am requesting a substantive response to that appeal, rather than immediate production of every potentially responsive document.

Given the passage of 18 business days without any communication, I respectfully request that your office:

Acknowledge receipt of my October 1, 2026, appeal.

Provide a written determination addressing the grounds raised in my appeal.

If the denial is maintained, identify the specific statutory provisions supporting continued withholding.

If additional time is necessary, explain the reason for the delay and provide a reasonable date by which a substantive determination will be issued.


The Open Records Act’s requirement of prompt, reasonable access is intended to ensure meaningful public oversight of government operations. An appeal of a denial should likewise receive timely consideration, particularly when the requested records concern the integrity and reliability of forensic evidence used in criminal proceedings.

I respectfully request a substantive written response within five business days of this correspondence.

I appreciate your attention to this matter and look forward to receiving your response consistent with the requirements and public policy underlying the Oklahoma Open Records Act.

Sincerely,

Jennifer Holtzclaw
